headline: Apple may have to allow 3rd-party app payments and Apple Pay rivals in UK
summary: Britain's antitrust regulator has proposed new rules that could force Apple to open up its ecosystem, allowing third-party payment options for apps and competing services to Apple Pay in the UK.
details: Britain's Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) has proposed new measures targeting Apple's ecosystem. These proposals aim to force Apple to allow developers to offer third-party payment options for in-app purchases and enable rival payment services to compete with Apple Pay in the UK.

The move follows an investigation into Apple's mobile browsers and cloud gaming, which concluded that Apple holds significant market power. The CMA believes these changes would foster greater competition and offer consumers more choice and potentially lower prices.

Currently, Apple mandates the use of its own in-app payment system, taking a commission of up to 30%. The proposed changes could significantly alter how developers monetize their apps and how users make payments on iOS devices in the UK.

headline_marked: [[Taiwan raids Supermicro]] and two supply-chain partners in widening Nvidia smuggling probe
headline: Taiwan raids Supermicro and two supply-chain partners in widening Nvidia smuggling probe
summary: The raids are part of Taiwan's first criminal investigation into the diversion of Nvidia AI chips to China, with Supermicro's shares falling 8% after the news.
details: Taiwan's Keelung District Prosecutors' Office raided Supermicro Computer's Taiwan office on Monday, along with the homes of six individuals and three affiliated company sites. This expands the island's first criminal investigation into the diversion of Nvidia AI chips to China. Supermicro's shares fell 8% in U.S. trading.

The probe also targeted Supermicro distributor Albatron Technology and data center operator Chief Telecom, according to sources. Albatron confirmed the search, reporting no financial or operational impact, while Chief Telecom stated its operations remained normal.

Taiwanese law currently doesn't classify the unauthorized export of AI chips to China as a crime. Prosecutors are using existing statutes, with previous raids leading to charges for falsifying shipping documents, not export breaches.

Authorities seized roughly 50 Supermicro servers bound for China, Hong Kong, and Macau in earlier raids. The six individuals questioned in the latest action are also facing inquiries over document offenses.

Taipei is considering new legislation to restrict AI chip sales to all customers in China, not just blacklisted firms. This change would allow prosecutors to charge smuggling as an export crime, aligning with U.S. efforts.

The U.S. is prosecuting a similar scheme under export-control law, with Supermicro co-founder Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw facing charges for allegedly conspiring to divert $2.5 billion in Nvidia-equipped servers to China. Liaw pleaded not guilty.

It's notable that Taiwan, a major manufacturer of advanced AI chips, has weaker legal mechanisms against unlawful diversion compared to the U.S. The GPUs are fabricated by TSMC in Taiwan before assembly into Supermicro servers.

Monday's raids mark the first time the distribution chain itself has been directly targeted, whereas previous efforts focused on executives accused of orchestrating the smuggling. Neither Albatron nor Chief Telecom has been charged yet.
